articles.title: 1 Realistic Blockbuster Trade That Should Happen Before NBA Season
articles.summary: At this point of the 2026 NBA offseason, there are mostly just a few T's to cross and a couple of I's to dot.
articles.body:
At this point of the 2026 NBA offseason, there are mostly just a few T's to cross and a couple of I's to dot.

Except for, you know, that 22-year-old All-NBA performer who remains without a deal.

That player is Jalen Duren, whose restricted free agency was unfortunately preceded by a big playoff flop—and a huge breakout season right before it.

Clearly, there have been complications in squaring both developments, to the point that negotiations between Duren and the Detroit Pistons have reportedly taken an "awfully nasty" turn, per ESPN's Tim MacMahon .

The gap between Duren's assessment of his value, fueled by that breakout, and Detroit's, shaped by his postseason struggles, may be too wide to bridge.

So, if the business of basketball has caused irreparable damage to this relationship, then a bold sign-and-trade might be the right business move to make.

Detroit Pistons receive: Ryan Rollins, Myles Turner and 2031 first-round pick (top-five protected)

Milwaukee Bucks receive: Jalen Duren (sign-and-trade)

They know he deftly handled a starring role in their most successful regular season in 20 years. They know he is a highly impactful presence on both ends and shares a close bond with franchise centerpiece Cade Cunningham.

And they know—or can at least reasonably project—that, at 22 years old, Duren's best seasons are still in front of him.

They also happen to know they aren't comfortable giving him the kind of contract he wants . Or maybe anything close to it. They also know their offense will face spacing concerns as long as Duren (0-for-6 from three in his career) shares a frontcourt with fellow building block Ausar Thompson (38-of-186).

They may have serious concerns about the long-term viability of this combo. They know they'd be locked into it if they met Duren's contract demands (or came close to them) and ironed out an extension with Thompson. And they know if they don't give Duren the offer he wants, they could lose control of this situation should he wind up signing the qualifying offer and thus paving a path to 2027 unrestricted free agency.

This deal offers a way out. Moreover, it just might help build a more cohesive lineup, even with Detroit trading away the most talented player in the exchange.

Myles Turner's blend of paint protection and floor spacing could create a more optimized frontcourt fit with Thompson. Ryan Rollins, meanwhile, spent his 2025-26 breakout looking every bit like the secondary scorer and shot-creator that Cunningham so badly needs alongside him. Only 13 players averaged 17 points, five assists and 2.5 three-pointers this past season; Rollins was one of them—and the second-youngest of the group.

Even if Turner is probably overpaid ( three years, $83.6 million left on his deal), and Rollins is responsible for only one notable season through four NBA campaigns, that's still a solid haul for someone the Pistons don't want to (over)pay. Especially when there's a lightly protected future first tacked on to help lessen the blow for fans who will struggle to figure out why their franchise, fresh off a 60-win effort, just cut ties with a 22-year-old All-Star.

As soon as Milwaukee split from Giannis Antetokounmpo this offseason, it got busy forming its next foundation. And honestly, it's possible this club's competitive window opens quicker than people think.

Hometown star Tyler Herro is a 26-year-old with a recent All-Star selection on his resume. Jaime Jaquez Jr. is a 25-year-old who was just runner-up for an end-of-season award . Even incoming lottery pick Brayden Burries is a soon-to-be 21-year-old whose scouting report featured NBA readiness among his greatest strengths.

If nothing else, this is a young core that could grow intriguing sooner than later—especially if the front office turbo-charged it with a talent like Duren.

While the Bucks would have to ink a sizable pact with the bouncy big man, the trade cost would look quite favorable for a 22-year-old star.

Turner, who will be 31 in March, underwhelmed during the first season of a big four-year contract. Rollins has proved little to this point beyond an ability to post big numbers on a 50-loss team.

Even that draft pick should not sting too badly, since the Bucks would still have Miami's 2031 first-rounder to dangle if they felt less bullish about their own long-term outlook.

That's not a nothing package, obviously, but it also isn't what you'd expect to see for a player as young and accomplished as Duren. Given what he and his team just achieved last season, he'd be a no-brainer keeper under almost any other circumstance. This contract stalemate, however, may have created an opportunity for the right buyer.

Why couldn't that be the Bucks? They aren't a free agent destination, so they'd only normally have access to a player like this by acing a draft pick. Duren fits Milwaukee's long-term timeline.

Plus, letting go of Rollins would give more clarity to a guard group that would still feature Herro, Burries, 2025 first-round pick Kasparas Jakučionis and 26-year-old Kevin Porter Jr., who just averaged 17.4 points and 7.4 assists.

Add Duren to this group, and the foundation would feel surprisingly solid for a franchise that just traded away its longtime face. Ace a couple of developmental projects (like Jakučionis, Nate Ament, Kel'el Ware and Ousmane Dieng), and the Bucks might be ready to rise right when several Eastern Conference elites start aging out of the top tier.

articles.title: 30 Overreactions to the 2026 NBA Offseason
articles.summary: Every NBA offseason has a different theme to it.
articles.body:
Every NBA offseason has a different theme to it.

This year's was a fun one: There was never a dull moment.

Just when you thought you might have all the splashes accounted for, something else would make a splash and send the basketball world into another reshuffling.

With action like this, imaginations are running wild about what all of this activity (or, in certain cases, inactivity) might mean for the short- and long-term future.

We can only guesstimate how things will go, which leads to a lot of overreactions. Like, say, one for all 30 teams.

Overreaction: The NBA has a new best defense.

The Hawks had last season's 10th-best defense ( fifth-best after Trae Young played his final game in Atlanta). This summer, they added 2024-25 All-Defensive first-teamer Lu Dort and fellow former shape-shifting member of the Oklahoma City Thunder Aaron Wiggins.

Couple them with what was already a wealth of defensive talent, and you're now looking at the league's stingiest defense, right?

Maybe , but let's see it in action before making such a definitive declaration. The Hawks should be all kinds of disruptive on defense. Sure, the Thunder still have a pretty terrific collection of stoppers, the San Antonio Spurs have that 7-foot-something alien everyone keeps talking about, and the Detroit Pistons employ a host of long-limbed, physical defenders.

The Hawks look poised to rank among the league's best defenses, but crowning them No. 1 already is an unnecessary rush to judgment.

The Celtics shattered expectations with a 56-win effort last season, and then promptly traded away the MVP candidate spawned during the campaign (Jaylen Brown, who landed sixth in MVP voting and second team All-NBA) for pennies on the dollar. Jayson Tatum is suddenly without a co-star, and that probably means Boston is out of the title race—for now.

The Celtics lack the high-end star power to contend for the crown right now, but they might only be an upgrade or two to rejoining the heavyweight contender ranks.

And since they have some wiggle room—a handful of first-round picks to throw around, some monster contracts coming off the books over the next few summers—they just might make those additions before the 28-year-old Tatum ages out of his prime.

Overreaction: They'll have the NBA's best backcourt in five years or less.

Those who kept an eye on Brooklyn's summer league squads surely had a chance to overindulge on optimism surrounding this year's No. 6 pick Mikel Brown Jr. and last year's No. 8 pick Egor Dëmin.

Between the former's flashy play style and the latter's ability to utilize his added muscle, they raised expectations by the minute and even gained a shared nickname along the way.

Excitement is fine (and fully warranted), but it still needs to stay within reason. This guard group has an undeniable chance to be awesome, but it remains only a possibility. Dëmin averaged 10.3 points on 39.9 percent shooting as a rookie, and Brown shot 41 percent during his lone season of college ball.

Their individual paths to stardom are steep.

Overreaction: They will regret dismantling their core.

The Hornets had a wholly ridiculous January to April stretch in which they went 33-16 with the league's best net rating ( plus-10.5 ). But they just snatched the wind from their own sails by jettisoning two key contributors (LaMelo Ball and Miles Bridges) in offseason trades.

And guess what? It was the right call. Ball, a walking injury risk with less than stellar play-style reviews , brought back Naz Reid, an unprotected first-round pick, three first-round swaps and three second-round picks.

Bridges, a volume scorer with a lot of hollow stats, somehow delivered an unprotected future first. The value was impossible to pass up, and they can now grow a more accommodating and sustainable core around cornerstones Kon Knueppel and Brandon Miller.

Overreaction: They blew their cap space on nothing.

This was supposed to be a transformational summer for the Bulls, and in certain ways, it was. Their front office got an overdue overhaul, and the draft lottery delivered a pair of possible building blocks (No. 4 pick Caleb Wilson and No. 15 pick Dailyn Swain). But the gobs of cap space they possessed wound up delivering only Nic Claxton, Norman Powell and Zach Collins (and hopes of a late Bennedict Mathurin addition). Yikes, right?

Well, sort of, but they had to find someone to man the middle and landed a perfectly suitable solution with the 27-year-old Claxton. And they needed someone to help pick up the scoring slack, and Powell, a 21-plus-point scorer the past two seasons, should be up to that challenge. Neither may stick around Chicago long, but that's probably the point—lean on the vets now as their prospects find their footing and then flip those players for more long-term assets when the youth is ready to take over.

Overreaction: They finally cracked the code at small forward.

Ever since Cleveland brought Donovan Mitchell to town, this organization has chased one possible solution at small forward after the next. Could that carousel finally stop spinning? That's surely the hope after this front office burned its remaining draft assets to be crowned surprise winners of the Peyton Watson sweepstakes.

This had to be encouraging, if only to see Cleveland do something in response to the many splashes made by fellow East elites. That said, it's not like Watson's arrival guarantees the Cavs finally have their missing piece at the 3. He is a stingy, disruptive defender, but his offense is very much a work in progress.

If he can't crank up the three-point volume while sustaining his newfound efficiency, it could be hard for this offense to breathe when he's slotting alongside Evan Mobley and Jarrett Allen.

Overreaction: This roster makes no sense.

The Mavericks' roster reads like it's stuck between two eras—probably because it is.

Kyrie Irving leads a veteran core that was initially brought together to give Luka Dončić a championship chance. Meanwhile, a young nucleus is starting to take shape around 2025 top pick Cooper Flagg. This group is also light on ball-handlers and heavier than it needs to be with forwards.

And yet, this might somehow be the right spot for the Mavericks at the moment. They're still figuring things out with Flagg, like how he'll fare alongside an established star like Irving (who missed all of last season while rehabbing a torn ACL).

They're also in no rush to move veterans ( other than perhaps Klay Thompson), since they could try to compete with them first, knowing they'll always maintain trade value.

Overreaction: They're giving Nikola Jokić reasons to consider leaving.

Setting aside any sentimental attachments or the desire to complete a career with one franchise, what is the great argument for Jokić recommitting to Denver ? The Nuggets are still a really good team, but is greatness a legitimate possibility? They've won two total playoff series in the three seasons since their 2023 title run, and their already compromised defense now must find a way to proceed without Peyton Watson.

All of this feels ominous, yet none of it really matters unless Jokić decides it does. And so far, nothing has changed the notion that he plans to continue his career in Denver. ( Well, nothing other than the dreams of hopeful poachers .) The Nuggets should be careful about taking his presence for granted, but it hardly sounds like he is scanning for the exits.

Overreaction: Cade Cunningham's co-star isn't coming.

The rumor mill connected the Pistons to some fascinating scenarios this summer, but nothing major materialized. Labeling their offseason dud is a bit harsh—John Collins can pile up points, and Isaiah Joe's shooting scratches a big itch—but it's certainly disappointing when weighed against some of those initial expectations, especially when nothing has been figured out with Jalen Duren yet.

This all leaves Cunningham without the co-star he seemingly needs to make a real championship push. Detroit will have more chances, though. If the Pistons can't develop that player (maybe Duren or Ausar Thompson), they'll still have the assets needed to go pursue a needle-mover in a trade.

Overreaction: They failed Stephen Curry.

As shepherds of Curry's once-in-a-lifetime career, the Warriors have some responsibility for ensuring he has a chance to play for something of significance. So, when they're effectively running back a 45-loss roster for what will be his age-38 season, it sure feels like a franchise-wide failure.

Maybe history will remember it as such, but Golden State still has a chance to field a more formidable supporting cast around him. It'll just take some time to make that happen. The Warriors have draft capital to throw around and navigable paths toward big-time financial flexibility, plus a potential difference-maker on the mend in Jimmy Butler, so things aren't nearly as dire as they may initially appear.

After following consecutive 52-win campaigns with first-round exits, the Rockets appeared open for anything this summer. They gave potential trade partners the impression that Amen Thompson was their "only near untouchable," per Yahoo Sports' Kelly Iko , suggesting their roster might look dramatically different for the 2026-27 season.

When considering the potential activity, this feels a lot closer to status quo. This is not, however, a stationary squad. Fred VanVleet is back, Marcus Smart and Bogdan Bogdanović have joined the party and the young core has had another offseason of development. Splash-less summer or not, it's still a collective stock up for Space City.

Overreaction: A sleepy summer has them set up for disappointment.

Tyrese Haliburton has wondered aloud why the league isn't treating his return from a torn Achilles as a bigger deal. Clearly, expectations in the Circle City are enormous with the franchise floor general back and Ivica Zubac manning the middle.

You wonder whether expectations will be too high, though, given all that has changed in the East since Indiana booked that surprise trip to the 2025 NBA Finals.

When players like Giannis Antetokounmpo, Jaylen Brown, LeBron James and (presumably) Kawhi Leonard are moving around, that activity tends to overshadow the return of a small-market's star. But Haliburton might be onto something.

This offense hums when he's at the helm, and Zubac can be a stabilizer at center. The Pacers didn't need a busy summer to drum up excitement (at least internally) around their chances for the upcoming campaign.

Overreaction: Keaton Wagler was exposed in Summer League.

With the Clippers in the process of closing out the Kawhi Leonard chapter, Wagler, their No. 5 pick, is prominently positioned for whatever comes next. So, he had plenty of eyeballs on him at summer league, and he didn't exactly thrive under the spotlight. He was an inefficient scorer and an ineffective contributor in virtually every other category.

It was disappointing to see. It was also potentially meaningless. Las Vegas has a history of fooling the hoops world with mirages . And Wagler, who impacts the game more with feel than freakish physical tools, never figured to thrive in that environment. You'd still prefer to see him star at summer league, but overreacting to the fact he didn't is pointless.

Overreaction: They just pumped all of their assets into a Play-In roster.

The Lakers prioritized a new contract for Austin Reaves and finding an impact center this offseason. They managed to check both boxes, but they paid an exorbitant cost to do it: $184.8 million for Reaves, and then two first-round picks and two first-round pick swaps for the right to give Walker Kessler $129.5 million.

Luka Dončić at least seems on board with the moves , but there isn't an obvious way for L.A. to wiggle out of this should things run awry.

And maybe that's OK. Dončić plus a second scorer and shot-creator has proved an awful potent combo in the past. Dončić plus an impact center has typically delivered results, too. If L.A. works some developmental magic on the likes of Cameron Carr, Adou Thiero and Quentin Grimes, this roster could surprise sooner than later.

Overreaction: Cameron Boozer should've been the No. 1 pick.

Did anyone catch Boozer's run with the summer-league Grizzlies? You might still be cleaning up drool puddles if you did. He was any and everything he was billed to be: versatile, productive, efficient and absolutely impactful on winning.

So, should he be cemented on way-too-early re-draft boards now? Nope. The skills he showed in summer league were never questioned; any knocks were always tied to the fact he lagged behind both AJ Dybantsa and Darryn Peterson in terms of physical tools, which is clearly still the case. Boozer might already have the highest floor of the three, but teams holding the No. 1 pick are seeking more than safety.

Overreaction: Landing a whale unlocks immediate championship possibilities.

For years, the Heat waited for this very opportunity—not simply landing a superstar, but getting Giannis freakin' Antetokounmpo. And given how successful they'd managed to be in some of those superstar-less seasons, his addition has to make them an immediate factor in the championship chase, right?

Well, you never want to rule out anything involving a player this talented, but this roster has question marks all around the Antetokounmpo-Bam Adebayo combo (which has its own logistical concerns with spacing). Throw in the rising tides of a fully loaded East, and Miami isn't guaranteed a top-six seed, much less a legitimate shot at winning it all.

Overreaction: They botched the Giannis Antetokounmpo blockbuster.

By the time the Bucks got around to trading away Antetokounmpo, he was entrenched as the best player in franchise history. And through that lens, Milwaukee's return package—Tyler Herro, Jaime Jaquez Jr., Kel'el Ware, Kasparas Jakučionis, three firsts, a swap and a second—might seem so underwhelming to make you think the Bucks really botched this.

They didn't. Or they didn't botch it this offseason, at least. Teams weren't beating that offer (especially if Milwaukee thinks the homegrown Herro is a keeper) for a 31-year-old with shooting limitations, contract uncertainty and some recent injury trouble. The Bucks just needed to rip this Band-Aid off sooner. Everyone outside of Milwaukee could see this coming and delaying the inevitable denied this club what could have been a truly ridiculous collection of incoming assets.

Overreaction: Anthony Edwards has a championship chance now.

The Wolves needed more consistent offensive support for Edwards and just found it in LaMelo Ball, a nightly 20-point, 10-assist threat with deep shooting range, two-steps-ahead passing vision and gobs of creativity. This was someone whom Minnesota's decision-makers "had long believed was the ideal backcourt running mate for Anthony Edwards," per The Athletic's Jon Krawczynski .

The Wolves' working theory is a fun one. It's also risky as heck. Minnesota effectively drained its asset pool and changed identities for an offense-leaning (or offense-only) player who owns a career 41.8 field-goal percentage and has reached the playoffs exactly zero times. Oh, and he has played fewer than 52 games in four of his six seasons. It would be objectively awesome if this works, but the list of reasons to believe it won't is not a short one.

Overreaction: They missed their window to reset.

Sellers were in top demand this offseason as there weren't enough impact players to satiate the many buyers. Shouldn't the Pelicans have used that to their advantage? Trey Murphy III and Herbert Jones should've had rich markets, and Zion Williamson might've even been movable after making 60-plus appearances for the second time in the last three seasons.

For whatever reason, though, the stars never aligned on a swap. Maybe that was a major misfire by New Orleans, but executive vice president of basketball operations Joe Dumars told NOLA.com's Rod Walker the inactivity was "not from a lack of effort or us deciding we didn't want to do anything." The Pelicans seemingly just didn't back down from the prices they set, and there's a chance their patience will be rewarded the next time trade season gets rolling.

Overreaction: Their roster won't be the same without Mitchell Robinson.

It could be ages before the Knicks wind up with a player as big and bouncy as Robinson. The 7-foot rim-runner may not have been the most durable player around, but he always made his presence felt in small doses. Despite often operating opposite New York's stacked starting lineup, Robinson managed to post a plus-2.6 net differential .

New York will miss Robinson's paint presence and anti-gravity ups, but not in a this-club-can't-repeat kind of way. The Knicks gave him fewer than 20 minutes in the regular season and trimmed that to less than 14 in the playoffs, so they're only filling a niche role. And Andre Drummond should be a serviceable replacement, especially on a minimum contract.

Overreaction: Dynasties are impossible in the NBA's economic environment.

The Thunder won 132 regular-season games and six playoff series over the past two seasons. They traded away three rotation regulars over the offseason, and not to accommodate newcomers but rather to make the budget more manageable. Such is life under this collective bargaining agreement.

Or is it? Because these maneuvers weren't apron-related. As The Athletic's Fred Katz relayed, "In the league's third-smallest market, owner Clay Bennett is sticking to a budget."

Other organizations won't give themselves the same restrictions, meaning their budgets could certainly stretch farther than this, especially if doing so meant keeping a potential dynasty together.

Overreaction: They're denying the reality of their wing tandem.

The Magic just played their fourth season with both Paolo Banchero and Franz Wagner on the wing. They even propped up that pairing with a bold (and budget-busting) trade for Desmond Bane. Yet, they're still awaiting the first playoff series win of the Banchero-Wagner era. Perhaps because this twosome just doesn't work.

But the Magic are right for thinking it's too soon to make that call. A coaching change could help better align the puzzle pieces. And there are still ways to tweak this core without demolishing the foundation. Teams rarely improve by trading their best players away.

Overreaction: This offense has too many mouths to feed.

Every time a superteam is spawned, the same concern rises shortly thereafter: There's only one basketball to go around . As if that reality doesn't exist for every other team in the Association.

Will it be simple to satisfy all four of LeBron James, Jaylen Brown, Tyrese Maxey and Joel Embiid? Nope—but that's a problem that just about every other franchise would love to try tackling.

"Talking to (head coach Nick Nurse), he's excited. It's just like a kid in a candy store," Sixers president of basketball operations Mike Gansey told reporters . "He's like, 'How are we going to put this thing together and see if it works?'"

When that one basketball goes around, it will often find its way to either a former MVP or a current All-NBA honoree. If Philly can strike the right balance, this offense should be silly.

Overreaction: Devin Booker still has no help.

The Suns stripped themselves of a Booker co-star when they traded Kevin Durant last offseason. At this rate, it doesn't feel like they're even searching for one. When they're adding talent, it's of the role-playing variety: Miles Bridges as a scoring forward, Luke Kennard as a net-shredder, Koa Peat as a forceful dot-connector.

Maybe this all means the whole outpaces the sum of the parts again. Phoenix overpaid for Bridges, but it did have a void to fill at power forward. It signed a lot of sensible contracts, which should remain movable if a direction change is needed. And things aren't even helpless on the co-star front, as big developmental leaps could still be in front of Jalen Green and Khaman Maluach, and the regression that was supposed to hit Dillon Brooks in the playoffs never came close to materializing.

The Blazers saw an offer they couldn't refuse. That's the only rationale that makes sense behind their summer swap of Jerami Grant and Kris Murray for Ja Morant. And honestly, that reasoning is sound. It's sort of a no-risk, all-reward wager on a two-time All-Star who just turned 27. In a vacuum, there's a lot to love.

Basketball teams don't play in a vacuum, though, and this is one situation where the old there's only one ball thing feels legitimately worrisome. How does a roster simultaneously squeeze the most out of Morant, Damian Lillard, Scoot Henderson and Jrue Holiday? And how does that guard group not totally torpedo the on-ball opportunities for All-Star swingman Deni Avdija? Even in a positionless league, there are too many cooks in this kitchen.

Overreaction: Darius Acuff Jr. is doomed.

Summer league was rough for Acuff. His scoring volume reached an acceptable level, but that was it for positives. His efficiency underwhelmed, his playmaking unraveled amid a sea of turnovers and his defense lived up to its unfavorable billing.

None of that necessarily matters, though. Acuff handled a heavy responsibility list as a teenager in a chaotic environment. Things going well may have been more surprising than these struggles.

As far as there are worries with Acuff, who won't turn 20 until November, they hinge more around his chances of germinating in what has been, shall we say, less than fruitful soil in Sacramento.

Overreaction: De'Aaron Fox has got to go.

The NBA Finals put the worst kind of spotlight onto Fox. He not only struggled in major moments, he also saw the player right behind him on the depth chart, last summer's No. 2 pick Dylan Harper, succeed in such a way that everyone wondered why he wasn't getting more minutes . The worst read on the situation painted Fox as a $221.7 million obstacle in San Antonio's path.

That's not at all how the Spurs see it, though. General manager Brian Wright expressed "the ultimate faith in De'Aaron," and The Athletic's Jared Weiss relayed that "multiple team and league sources said the Spurs still see Fox as a critical piece of the team's future." This is how San Antonio needs to handle this, since it has enough floor time and touches to get the best out of its three-headed monster in the backcourt, and it needs the on-court organization Fox offers.

Overreaction: Summer League proved Allen Graves was a steal.

Graves was a curiosity in college, a reserve on a mid-major with some of the best analytics around. Toronto snatched him up with this summer's 19th pick, and he immediately showcased his versatility on the summer circuit: 16.8 points, 6.8 rebounds, 3.0 assists and 2.3 steals across four contests.

It was a proof-of-concept performance for everyone who saw him as a potential Swiss Army knife.

It was also maybe indicative of nothing for his future. His lack of athleticism could be a real challenge against actual NBA defenders, and his outside shooting still has to prove sustainable with a significant increase in volume.

This isn't to say Toronto fans should abandon hope. It's just a reminder that those hopes are nothing more than that at this stage.

Overreaction: Darryn Peterson isn't a playmaker.

Peterson's improvement as a playmaker in high school played a big part in his standing as a top 2026 draft prospect. Then, he went to Kansas and totaled exactly as many turnovers as assists (38 each) in 24 games. Next, he technically fared slightly better at Sacramento—26 assists against 24 turnovers in five outings.

This could be a cause for major concern, but it's too early to really raise that alarm. For one, he could star without a ton of passing production as an all-purpose shotmaker in a multi-distributor offense. Second, he showed advanced passing reads as a prep star, and he might just need better health and superior scoring help around him to get back into that bag.

After three straight seasons with 64-plus losses, the Wizards are putting their losing ways behind them. Washington has organically grown a compelling young core and then supplemented it with established stars (Trae Young, Anthony Davis) and the No. 1 pick in a highly celebrated draft (AJ Dybantsa).

The Wizards even brought back Khris Middleton and turned their attention toward DeMar DeRozan after a failed courtship of Russell Westbrook.

Clearly, Washington thinks it is ready to turn the corner. A bit of brake-pumping feels warranted. Young is a one-way contributor, Davis can't stay on the court (and isn't a lock to stick around) and this young nucleus has won nothing at this level.

The future is bright—there's no denying that—but Washington may not be out of the woods just yet.

articles.title: Watch Caitlin Clark, 'Ted Lasso' Star Jason Sudeikis Embrace in New Video After Fever's Win vs. Sky
articles.summary: Indiana Fever star Caitlin Clark and actor Jason Sudeikis had a quick chat following Indy's 113-90 win over the Chicago Sky on Sunday.
articles.body:
Indiana Fever star Caitlin Clark and actor Jason Sudeikis had a quick chat following Indy's 113-90 win over the Chicago Sky on Sunday.

The Ted Lasso star was on hand to watch Clark drop 37 points and 10 assists for one of her best performances of the 2026 WNBA season.

With the victory, Indiana improved to 25-14. The Fever remain fifth in the standings but only trail the second-place Golden State Valkyries by 1.5 games.

articles.title: No Issues for Sophie Cunningham and DiJonai Carrington as Fever Beat Sky in Rematch
articles.summary: CHICAGO (AP) — The rematch was no big deal.
articles.body:
CHICAGO (AP) — The rematch was no big deal.

There were no major issues for Sophie Cunningham and DiJonai Carrington in Indiana's 113-90 victory over Chicago on Sunday night. Cunningham scored three points for the Fever in 11 minutes, and Carrington had seven points for the Sky in 18 minutes.

It was the first matchup between the teams since Cunningham was taken down by Carrington on a fast break earlier this month. Carrington was listed as questionable with a left foot injury, but she was cleared after going through warmups.

Enes Kanter Freedom Ejected from WNBA Game

Cunningham downplayed any lingering animosity between the teams going into the game. Indiana had dropped two in a row.

"My mindset has never changed. I think it is what it is," Cunningham said. "I'm locked in on tonight. ... I think we're just out here trying to get the win."

Cunningham and Carrington both checked in for the first time with 3:04 left in the first quarter. There were no disputes of note between the two players all night long.

Sky coach Tyler Marsh said he didn't have any conversations with his players before the game about the charged atmosphere for their previous matchup.

"That kind of was what it was last game and anything that came out of it kind of lasted for that time," Marsh said. "But for us, again, it was on to the next one in front of us."

Cunningham was going up for a layup in the first quarter of Indiana's 90-86 win on Aug. 8 when Carrington came from behind and hit her in the head and neck, knocking her to the court as the shot went in. Cunningham got up, charged Carrington and pushed her as she was held back by a teammate.

The play was reviewed and upgraded to a Flagrant 2 after the referee said there was windup, impact and follow-through on the foul, resulting in Carrington's ejection.

Shortly after she was thrown out, Carrington posted "WHITE PRIVILEGE" on social media and tagged the Fever. Carrington is Black and Cunningham is white.

Days later, Carrington posted that she never claimed the assessment of the Flagrant 2 was the result of white privilege, but she didn't elaborate any further.

"I (couldn't) care less about what she does, what she tweets, any of that," Cunningham said before Sunday's game. "I'm here to play basketball.

"There's going to be people who are going to talk about it ... but to me, it's just another basketball game."

articles.title: 2025 NBA Contenders Who Need a Trade Most
articles.summary: The NBA trade deadline is fast approaching, and the wheeling and dealing has already begun ahead of February 6.
articles.body:
The NBA trade deadline is fast approaching, and the wheeling and dealing has already begun ahead of February 6.

The Los Angeles Lakers, Golden State Warriors and Phoenix Suns have made moves. And there could be a lot of movement in the coming weeks as teams load up for playoff runs.

Many players could be on the move. The Brooklyn Nets, Utah Jazz and Portland Trail Blazers could be sellers at this draft.

Of course, the Jimmy Butler trade demand hangs over the Miami Heat. The Suns are interested in moving Bradley Beal with his pesky no-trade clause. Zach LaVine's name continues to be thrown into trade rumors. Cameron Johnson's name is burning up the phone lines (he'll be mentioned a lot below).

Several teams need to make trades. Some of these moves can turn teams into contenders or strengthen contenders.

It's been an interesting season for the Sacramento Kings.

At one point, they looked like sellers at the deadline, with some De'Aaron Fox unhappiness. That resulted in the firing of head coach Mike Brown. Since then, the team has caught fire under Doug Christie. The Kings are now buyers in the trade marketplace.

Based on how the Kings have been playing since the coaching change, they should be considered a contender. Under Christie, they have the second-best win percentage in the NBA, just behind Oklahoma City. However, they do need a three-and-D wing player with more of an emphasis on shooting.

Adding another shooter to the roster will create more driving lanes for Fox, DeMar DeRozan and Malik Monk. The Kings are 22nd in three-point attempts and 20th in three-point percentage.

There were rumors that Sacramento already inquired about the Brooklyn Nets' Cameron Johnson. No deal seems imminent between the two teams, but it does show what the Kings will be looking for on the market.

Several contenders will be looking for players like Johnson. The Los Angeles Lakers already took Dorian Finney-Smith off the market. The Kings are playing great basketball, 11-4 over their last 15 games. If Sacramento wants to jump into the contender tier, it needs to make a trade at this deadline and cannot stand pat.

After a woeful start to the season, the Milwaukee Bucks have stabilized and are sitting fourth in the Eastern Conference. Giannis Antetokounmpo has been a dominant force, averaging 31.5 points and 12.2 rebounds a game. Damian Lillard has found his groove from three after the dip last season. Even with the duo rolling, the Bucks must move by February 6th.

This was supposed to be a trio though, Khris Middleton has been held back by injuries. His scoring is down again this season after returning to the court in December. The Bucks need a third star on the wing. Preferably someone who can also help bolster their porous perimeter defense.

The Bucks have been at the center of several rumors, from interest in Jimmy Butler to a possible Bradley Beal or Zach LaVine landing spot and everything in between. Beal and LaVine won't help with their perimeter defensive issues, but their ability to score offensively can offset the Bucks's weakness there.

The Bucks need a shot in the arm to help attack the Cleveland Cavaliers, Boston Celtics, and New York Knicks. They are 0-8 against the top teams in the East. The Bucks have to take a swing to have a true shot at taking down any of the top three in the conference.

Everyone's heads turned when the Golden State Warriors started 12-3 this season. Then, the wheels fell off the wagon, and the Warriors have gone 10-20 since that start. One can argue that maybe they should have found a deal for Lauri Markkanen in the offseason, as we rumored, but that ship has sailed. They cannot miss the boat this time around.

Golden State made a trade, bringing in Dennis Schroder from the Brooklyn Nets. Adding another ball handler to the roster was a smart move, but more importantly, they made the trade early enough that Schroder could be included in another trade by deadline day.

The Warriors desperately need to add someone who could take some of the scoring pressure off Stephen Curry. There is not a reliable second option on the roster; some nights, it is Andrew Wiggins, Jonathan Kuminga (who has been injured since 1/5), and Buddy Hield. That is not good enough.

The real problem for the Warriors is that the options for a second option that are available are not earth-shattering. LaVine, Beal, and even Butler are interesting names, but the price tag will be too high for the Warriors. Brandon Ingram from New Orleans is available, but he is currently injured, does not have a great history with Steve Kerr stemming from his Team USA run, and will be looking for a big contract in the offseason.

The Warriors' options are not great. It might be better to sit out this trade deadline, but doing that will be punting on this season. If Golden State cannot find a solid second consistent scorer, they are wasting another Curry season, and that is unforgivable.

Before discussing what the Memphis Grizzlies should do this deadline, let's take a quick look back. It was not that long ago that Memphis looked like they were going to conquer the Western Conference.

Everyone knows what happened next, but most don't remember that the Grizzlies made a run at a wing/forward at the 2023 deadline. The price for OG Anunoby was too high for Memphis, but it will remain a fun what-if.

This time, with the deadline approaching, the Grizzlies' standing in the league is different, but their need is very similar. They are just a half-game out of second in the West but do not have full contender status. To get there, Memphis needs to add offensive and defensive firepower.

The Grizzlies should be in the market for a player similar to Anunoby. Cam Johnson should be a target for Memphis, putting them on that contender track. The price the Toronto Raptors were asking for in 2023 was high. It is rumored that the Brooklyn Nets are seeking two first-round picks for Johnson, which are lower than the price of Anunoby in the past.

If the Grizzlies' chase for Johnson is too much, they should look at other targets, like maybe Jerami Grant in Portland. They can also take a flyer on Kyle Kuzma, who is having a down year and could be in need of a change of scenery.

Memphis needs to level up if it is going to compete with the Oklahoma City Thunder, and its best chance is to make a move at the deadline.

articles.title: DeWanna Bonner Lands Mercury Contract Buyout, Top Landing Spots for WNBA Star Amid Playoff Race
articles.summary: The Phoenix Mercury announced Monday that they bought out six-time All-Star DeWanna Bonner.
articles.body:
The Phoenix Mercury announced Monday that they bought out six-time All-Star DeWanna Bonner.

General manager Nick U'Ren said the move "gives her the opportunity to chase a title in what could be her final postseason" as the Mercury have already been eliminated from playoff contention.

Bonner's agent Mike Cound praised the Mercury after the move.

"They were great," Cound told Kareem Copeland of ESPN. "Many teams in the league wouldn't consider this, but this is a special circumstance and Phoenix is a very player-friendly organization. She's really appreciative of them."

Bonner averaged 10.6 points and 6.1 rebounds in 38 games with the team.

Any move to a contender will be complicated by the WNBA's hard salary cap and 12-player roster maximum. In terms of team needs and looking at the standings, the Las Vegas Aces, Dallas Wings and Washington Mystics all make sense.

The reigning WNBA champions are third in the league and now have a void in the frontcourt with NaLyssa Smith suffering a knee injury in in Sunday's 88-78 win over the Toronto Tempo.

Chalk it up to pure coincidence or fate, but Las Vegas could've seen one of its starters go down for the season and a prospective replacement emerge all within the space of 24 hours.

The Mystics and Wings are in similar positions in that they have emergent squads another year or two from seriously contending for a title.

In the case of Washington, Bonner would provide invaluable experience. Betnijah Laney-Hamilton is the only player on the active roster older than 27. That the Mystics are a playoff team while relying on so much youth is an achievement on its own.

Dallas has taken a big step forward in Paige Bueckers' second season.

The Wings showed ambition by poaching Jessica Shepard and co-Defensive Player of the Year Alanna Smith from the Minnesota Lynx. Shepard has exceeded expectations by making her first All-Star team, but Smith has seriously regressed. Bonner might make up some of the difference.

The Atlanta Dream could be in the mix, too.

From Bonner's perspective, they'd be more attractive than Dallas or Washington, and they've seen two key contributors in their frontcourt struggle to match their 2025 production. Naz Hillmon isn't the three-point threat she was en route to being Sixth Player of the Year, and Brionna Jones hasn't recaptured her All-Star form after suffering a torn meniscus while playing overseas.

Bonner turned 39 a few days ago and she's clearly no longer at her peak. She's still playing at a level that will make her useful for a top-eight team in the WNBA.

articles.title: 'Sugar to S--t,' LaVar Ball Trolls Hornets After LaMelo Was Traded to Wolves

articles.body:
The Charlotte Hornets opted to trade star point guard LaMelo Ball to the Minnesota Timberwolves this offseason, and LaVar Ball thinks his son's former team is in for a rough year.

LaVar said on Ultimate Dads Unplugged that he thinks the Hornets are going to "go from sugar to s--t real quick," but he's ultimately happy with the move because it gives LaMelo the chance to compete for a title.

"When he was on there, I told him two things. I said, 'Yo, you ain't never win no championship just with Melo by himself. What you must do is get is get his two brothers or trade him.' And they traded him the next day, so it's all good," he said (12:10 mark).

Offseason Overreactions for Every Team 🫨

Jayson Tatum's dad blunt about Celtics roster

The Hornets traded LaMelo to Minnesota in return for Naz Reid, an unprotected first-round pick in 2033, three first-round pick swaps in 2028, 2029 and 2030, and three second-round picks in 2029, 2032 and 2033.

The move perhaps indicated that Charlotte is shifting towards building around Brandon Miller and Kon Knueppel.

LaMelo is coming off a season in which he put up 20.1 points, 7.1 assists and 4.8 rebounds per game, marking one of the best years of his career. The Hornets were close to sneaking into the playoffs for the first time in years, but they still decided it was time to move on.

Whether they made the right call to trade LaMelo remains to be seen, but LaVar believes they'll regret it.

articles.title: Jugar la SuperCup tiene premio: esto es lo que se llevarán los participantes
articles.standfirst: La nueva competición de la Euroliga tendrá lugar en Abu Dabi los días 18 y 19 de septiembre
articles.summary: La nueva competición de la Euroliga tendrá lugar en Abu Dabi los días 18 y 19 de septiembre
articles.body: Los próximos días 18 y 19 el baloncesto europeo verá nacer una nueva competición. Se trata de la SuperCup de la Euroliga, un torneo que vale como pretemporada para los equipos pero que, dado el nivel de los rivales, se puede considerar un competición más, con un título en juego, y con mucho prestigio para repartir. Y el prestigio no será lo único que se reparta. Jugar la SuperCup tiene premio económico para los cuatro equipos que estarán presentes en el Etihad Arena de Abu Dabi. Además de presentar un cartel con cuatro equipos que estarán luchando por llegar a la Final Four en mayo, los participantes de la SuperCup se llevarán un pico por tratar de ganar el primer título continental en juego. Los cuatro equipos participantes, Olympiacos (campeón), Real Madrid (subcampeón), Fenerbahce (campeón del año anterior) y Dubai Basketball (anfitrión), se llevarán 500.000 euros cada uno, sólo por estar en Abu Dabi esos dos días. El ganador final podrá aumentar la bolsa a unos 750.000 euros en total. Además, de lo ingresado, la Euroliga utilizará el resto para gastar en el evento y para aumentar la distribución económica a todos los equipos. En materia de entradas el abanico de precios es muy grande. Están las más económicas, que salen por unos 134 euros, y las más caras, la de primera fila, que ya se van a 2.547 euros, que contempla un paquete VIP. Entre medias ha varios precios, dependiendo del lugar en el pabellón. La Euroliga ya ha puesto las entradas a la venta desde este lunes en un paquete para los dos días. El 31 de agosto saldrán a la venta las entradas por día, permitiendo al aficionado acudir a los partidos del viernes o del sábado. En ese sentido, la entradas ya van desde la más barata, 55 euros hasta los 138 euros del viernes, o el tramo entre 102 y 256 para los del sábado dependiendo de la localidad en el pabellón.

articles.body: El Baskonia ha llegado a un acuerdo para fichar a Kenneth Faried, tal y como ha informado el periodista Chema de Lucas. Es un fichaje necesario para el equupo vitoriano que está tratando de recomponer su juego interior tras la marcha de jugadores como Eugene Omoruyi y, sobre todo, Mamadi Diakite. De hecho, Kenneth Faried no será el último interior que fiche el equipo azulgrana que buscará otro pívot más en el mercado. Faried se unirá como novedad en el Baskonia a los ya fichados Damion Baugh, DJ Stewart, Chris Duarte, A.J. Lawson. Faried, conocido como 'Manimal', jugó el pasado año en el Panathinaikos en su segunda experiencia en la Euroliga. En realidad firmó por dos meses para paliar la plaga de lesiones del equipo griego y acabó completando toda la temporada. Eso sí, su irrupción fue colosal y fue perdiendo fuerza a medida que avanzaba la campaña hasta contar muy poco para Ergin Ataman. Faried arrancó la Euroliga con tanta fuerza que fue elegido MVP del mes de noviembre. Acabó la pasada temporada con 5,8 puntos y 3,9 rebotes en 13 minutos en 35 partidos. articles.title: Shaedon Sharpe Suffers Significant Knee Injury, Latest Updates and Timeline for Blazers SG
articles.summary: The Portland Trail Blazers will be without a key starter for much of the 2026-27 campaign.
articles.body:
The Portland Trail Blazers will be without a key starter for much of the 2026-27 campaign.

Per ESPN's Shams Charania, shooting guard Shaedon Sharpe suffered a torn meniscus in his knee and is expected to miss six months.

The injury comes after the best season of Sharpe's career, in which he put up 20.8 points per game in his fourth year in the league. While he had a tremendous start to the 2025-26 campaign, he suffered an injury in February that forced him to miss more than two months of action.

He played significantly fewer minutes in the playoffs than he did during the regulars eason, averaging 13.6 minutes per game in the first round against the San Antonio Spurs and posting just 7.2 points per game.

That drop in minutes was perhaps more of a matchup decision than a slight to Sharpe, but it still likely left the young player hungry to prove he could provide solid minutes in the playoffs.

Unfortunately, he won't get to build off of the momentum from last season early in the 2026-27 campaign. If Sharpe's timeline is accurate, he wouldn't be back on the court until late February, meaning he'll have to make the most of the second half of the season and hope the Blazers are in a position to make the playoffs.

Even with Sharpe out for most of the year, Portland should be able to put together a solid season. The team has Deni Avdija leading the way and added star point guard Ja Morant this offseason.

The Blazers will also get Damian Lillard back after he missed all of last season.

Still, Portland can't afford any more injuries, but unfortunately, many of its players have a history of long-term ailments.

articles.title: Enes Kanter Freedom and Royce White Are Not Eligible for the WNBA Draft, AP Source Says
articles.summary: NEW YORK (AP) — Former NBA players Enes Kanter Freedom and Royce White are not eligible for the WNBA draft, a person familiar with the decision said Monday.
articles.body:
NEW YORK (AP) — Former NBA players Enes Kanter Freedom and Royce White are not eligible for the WNBA draft, a person familiar with the decision said Monday.

The person spoke to The Associated Press on condition of anonymity because of the sensitive nature of the situation. The person did not elaborate on the reasons for declaring the two men ineligible.

Freedom and White have declared their intention to enter next year's draft, but the WNBA has not publicly addressed their eligibility.

The WNBA has been the subject of recent debates on whether transgender women — people assigned male at birth who transition to align with their gender identity — should be allowed to participate in the league. There has never been such a player in the WNBA.

Although the league's collective bargaining agreement says the WNBA is restricted to women, it contains no more specific language about gender identity or sex assigned at birth. When they announced their intention to enter the draft, Freedom and White said they identified as women.

The 6-foot-10, 250-pound Freedom played 11 seasons in the NBA. White played in three NBA games.

Freedom was ejected from Sunday night's Indiana-Chicago game after he was confronted by Sky guard Natasha Cloud late in the third quarter.

Freedom was sitting along the baseline wearing a black shirt that read "WOMAN noun. adult human female."

The Fever called for a timeout after Cloud scored inside with 1:22 left in the third. Cloud then did a chest bump with teammate Aicha Coulibaly before turning around and walking in Freedom's direction.

Cloud, 34, started yelling and pointing at Freedom, 34, as she approached him. A standing Freedom held his arms out and took one step on the court as security and a handful of Sky players moved in between the two.

Freedom stopped near the basket to plead his case to security as he was escorted from the court area. He spun around while holding his shirt out and encouraged the crowd to respond as he walked toward the front lobby.

He had a conversation with a group of police officers before departing Wintrust Arena.

"I just got kicked out of a @WNBA game for supporting WOMEN!" Freedom wrote on social media Sunday night. "Let that sink in, AMERICA!"

Cloud met with team and league security after the game. She did not speak with the media.

Fever guard Sophie Cunningham said in an ESPN profile published last month that she was opposed to transgender girls and women competing in girls' and women's sports, and since then the league has been embroiled in debates about transgender participation. Freedom joined a small rally in support of Cunningham outside the arena before the game.

articles.title: R.J. Luis Jr. Cleared by Judge to Play for LSU After Spending Time with 2 NBA Teams
articles.summary: BATON ROUGE, La. (AP) — RJ Luis Jr., a former St. John's standout who recently signed with LSU after spending time with two NBA clubs, was cleared by a court Monday evening to start practicing and potentially play for the Tigers this season.
articles.body:
BATON ROUGE, La. (AP) — RJ Luis Jr., a former St. John's standout who recently signed with LSU after spending time with two NBA clubs, was cleared by a court Monday evening to start practicing and potentially play for the Tigers this season.

Luis, who briefly was under contract with the Utah Jazz and Boston Celtics but never played in an NBA game, hugged LSU coach Will Wade after the ruling by East Baton Rouge Parish District Court judge Ronald R. Johnson.

After a five-hour hearing, Johnson granted the player's request for a preliminary injunction against the NCAA, which had argued Luis was unlikely to win reinstatement after leaving college to turn pro in 2025.

"This is precedent. It's monumental," said Baton Rouge-based attorney Tony Clayton, who represented Luis along with Elliot Abrams of Raleigh, North Carolina. "This allows him to go practice, go play and we'll let the legal process work itself out."

The timeline for that process was not immediately clear.

"I don't know, but there's a lot of discovery that Elliot and I have to obtain," Clayton said. "We've got a lot of questions."

Luis' attorneys noted that the NCAA had granted exceptions allowing numerous players from overseas professional leagues to join college basketball programs, and argued that American players must be afforded the same opportunity.

They stressed that Luis not only had never played in an NBA game, but also had not played for the Celtics' G League affiliate because of an injury, and had far less of a professional basketball resume than numerous college players who'd been recruited from abroad.

NCAA attorney Taylor Askew argued that Luis' situation was not comparable to those who played for the developmental squads of pro organizations overseas because Luis chose to leave college for the NBA.

Askew noted that the only player in a similar situation to Luis was Alabama's Charles Bediako, who won a temporary retraining order allowing him to play five games for Alabama last season before an Alabama judge ultimately sided with NCAA assertions that he was ineligible.

"I understand Mr. Luis is disappointed that he was not drafted and did not play in the NBA as much as he would have liked," Askew said. "Actions have consequences. Decisions have outcomes and they're not always the right ones or the ones that you want."

As he made his ruling, Johnson said, "In the court's mind, (Luis) did not actually play professional basketball," and that whether Luis was properly advised of his options at the time he left college "lingers heavily before this court."

articles.title: Una camiseta de Jordan podría ser el objeto deportivo más valioso de la historia: ¡100 millones de dólares!
articles.standfirst: El 15 de septiembre se subasta la prenda que el mito vistió en el tercer partido de la final de 1998, cuando conquistó su sexto anillo con los Bulls antes de retirarse
articles.summary: El 15 de septiembre se subasta la prenda que el mito vistió en el tercer partido de la final de 1998, cuando conquistó su sexto anillo con los Bulls antes de retirarse
articles.body: La camiseta que Michael Jordan utilizó en el tercer partido de la final de la NBA en 1998 podría convertirse en el objeto más valioso en la historia del deporte. Se pondrá a subasta el 15 de septiembre y es posible que alcance los ¡100 millones de dólares! Se trata de la camiseta blanca que el mito usó en el tercer encuentro de la serie ante los Jazz. Además de ser uno de sus últimos partidos con los Bulls, durante la temporada de su 'Last dance', la vistió en una cita que terminó con el marcador de 96-54. Para hacer aún más única a la prenda, esos 42 puntos son la mayor diferencia en un partido de las finales de la NBA. Aquel 7 de junio, dado el amplio margen en el marcador, Jordan jugó sólo 32 minutos, su cifra más baja en aquellos playoffs, y metió 24 puntos. El actual propietario de la camiseta es el inversor deportivo y actor Rob Gough, que llegó a ella hace años a través de distintos intermediarios sin llegar a conocer a quien realmente la poseía. Él tiene otras piezas históricas que vistieron mitos como Kobe Bryant, Wilt Chamberlain, Tom Brady y Wayne Gretzky. "Se trata de conseguir piezas que se encuentren en la intersección del mejor atleta, el mejor escenario y un momento decisivo", asegura. Ahora la pone a subasta porque cree que no estaba siendo valorada como merece. "Tengo muchas obras de arte estupendas. Y cuando la gente viene a casa, se las salta para ir directamente a la camiseta. Fue entonces cuando me di cuenta de que esto es el nuevo arte moderno", cuenta Gough. Otra camiseta de Jordan, utilizada en el primer encuentro de aquellas finales de la NBA de 1998 fue vendida por 10,1 millones de dólares en 2022. Sin embargo, los Bulls cayeron en aquel encuentro por 88-85 después de una prórroga. "Yo no compro piezas de partidos en los que un jugador pierde porque uno piensa: 'Esa camiseta en la pared, ¿recuerdan cuando Michael Jordan perdió ese partido?' Simplemente no se dice eso", sentencia. Gough ya se hizo un nombre en la industria de los objetos de colección después de comprar una rara tarjeta de la estrella del béisbol Mickey Mantle de 1952 por 5,2 millones de dólares en 2021.

articles.title: Anthony Edwards tendrá que pagar 14.000 dólares al mes por mantener a un hijo al que no piensa conocer
articles.standfirst: La estrella de los Wolves tuvo en 2024 tres hijos con tres mujeres distintas
articles.summary: La estrella de los Wolves tuvo en 2024 tres hijos con tres mujeres distintas
articles.body: Los problemas extradeportivos vuelven a acuciar a Anthony Edwards. El escolta de los Timberwolves tendrá que pagar 14.000 dólares al mes en concepto de manutención para un hijo nacido en 2023 al que, según admitió bajo juramento, no conoce en persona y con el que renuncia a cualquier derecho a pasar tiempo con él. La cantidad a pagar, según informa el medio estadounidense TMZ, se determinó en función de los ingresos del jugador, una de las grandes estrellas de la NBA, que la próxima temporada ganará 48,9 millones de dólares. A ello se añade una póliza de seguro de vida que debe ser contratada por valor de 2,6 millones de dólares con la madre del niño como beneficiaria. Edwards ha protagonizado varios escándalos de relaciones personales con demandas por paternidad. En 2024, el escolta de los Wolves fue padre en tres ocasiones con tres mujeres distintas. Hace tiempo, ya había recibido la orden de pagar 3.000 dólares a la madre de otra niña. En diciembre de 2023, salieron a la luz los lamentables mensajes que el jugador envió a una modelo en los que le pedía que abortara. "Diablos, no puedo hacerlo", "no quiero niños" o "hazte un aborto jajaja", eran algunas de las frases que escribió Edwards, que también habría hecho a la mujer una transferencia de 100.000 dólares para llevar a cabo el procedimiento. Posteriormente, tuvo que disculparse públicamente por todo ello. A lo largo de la historia de la NBA, son muchos los jugadores que, pese a haber ganado grandes cantidades de dinero, se han visto arruinados, entre otras razones, por tener que mantener a su descendencia. Edwards, que todavía tiene 25 años, parece no ir por buen camino.

articles.standfirst: El pívot de 36 años y 2,05 metros jugó 478 encuentros entre Nuggets, Nets y Rockets y la temporada pasada militó en el Panathinaikos
articles.summary: El pívot de 36 años y 2,05 metros jugó 478 encuentros entre Nuggets, Nets y Rockets y la temporada pasada militó en el Panathinaikos
articles.body: El veterano Kenneth Faried reforzará la próxima temporada el juego interior de Kosner Baskonia, tras disputar la Euroliga con el Panathinaikos. El pivot norteamericano de 2.05 metros y 36 años cuenta con una amplia experiencia con más de 450 partidos de NBA donde llegó tras jugar en la NCAA, en la filas de Morehead State Eagles. Jugó 7 temporadas en Denver Nuggets y fue internacional con la selección estadounidense, con la que ganó el campeonato del mundo en 2014. Posteriormente, continuó su carrera en Brooklyn Nets, Capitanes de la Liga mexicana o CSKA Moscú, donde debutó en la máxima competición europea en la campaña 2021-22. La pasada campaña, en las filas del Panathinaikos, logró convertirse en el MVP del mes de noviembre en la Euroliga. "Con su incorporación, el club azulgrana suma experiencia y físico a sus filas para la temporada 2026-27", indicaron desde el club en una nota de prensa. El curso pasado firmó 5,2 puntos y 3,7 rebotes en los 35 duelos que disputó con el conjunto griego.

articles.title: Jassel Pérez, ritmo y talento ofensivo para el FIATC Girona
articles.standfirst: El escolta de 24 años y 1,90 metros llega al conjunto catalán tras ganar la Liga de Puerto Rico con Vaqueros de Bayamón promediando 18,9 puntos en playoffs
articles.summary: El escolta de 24 años y 1,90 metros llega al conjunto catalán tras ganar la Liga de Puerto Rico con Vaqueros de Bayamón promediando 18,9 puntos en playoffs
articles.body: El escolta dominicano Jassel Pérez se ha convertido este martes en nuevo jugador del FIATC Girona, que le ha hecho un contrato para las dos próximas temporadas, según ha anunciado el club catalán. Pérez, de 24 años y 1,90 metros, llegará a Fontajau justo después de proclamarse campeón de la liga de Puerto Rico con la camiseta de los Vaqueros de Bayamón. Allí ha promediado 21,4 puntos, 4 rebotes y 3,3 asistencias por partido en la fase regular y 18,9 puntos, 5,3 rebotes y 4,4 asistencias en las eliminatorias al título. La temporada pasada jugó primero en la Primera Federación con el Grupo Alega Cantabria (15,1 puntos, 4,1 rebotes y 3,3 asistencias) y desde diciembre en la Liga Endesa con el Coviran Granada, con el que disputó 23 partidos y promedió 11,3 puntos y 3,8 rebotes. Jassel Pérez es "una pieza necesaria" que "encaja perfectamente" en el estilo del FIATC Girona, según ha asegurado su director deportivo, Fernando San Emeterio en unas declaraciones distribuidas por el club catalán. "Tiene un talento natural y una exuberancia física que le hace diferencial a campo abierto, sobre todo en el momento de atacar el aro. También es capaz de defender muy bien porque es muy proactivo", ha añadido. San Emeterio también ha afirmado que el nuevo fichaje es "un jugador en clara progresión" que ha evolucionado en los dos últimos años y que es "muy humilde" y tiene "hambre de crecer y competir".

articles.title: New Kyrie Irving Trade Rumors Reveal Rivals 'Wonder Aloud' About Mavs Star's Availability
articles.summary: Despite the Dallas Mavericks declaring that they plan to retain star point guard Kyrie Irving during the 2026-27 season, it sounds like other teams aren't convinced they will keep their word.
articles.body:
Despite the Dallas Mavericks declaring that they plan to retain star point guard Kyrie Irving during the 2026-27 season, it sounds like other teams aren't convinced they will keep their word.

According to NBA insider Marc Stein , rival teams "continue to wonder aloud about how firmly Dallas will stick to that stance once the season begins and the next in-season trade deadline on Feb. 11 gradually approaches."

Offseason Overreactions for Every Team 🫨

Upon his hiring in May, new Mavs president of basketball operations Masai Ujiri made it clear that the team hoped to have Irving leading the way alongside 2025 No. 1 pick and reigning NBA Rookie of the Year Cooper Flagg.

"There's a huge curiosity in our minds to see how Kyrie fits playing with Flagg," Ujiri said at the time . "He's just that kind of incredible talent and player. And I think we owe that to this organization."

When the Mavs hired Dusty May as their new head coach the following month, May also declared that he was looking forward to working with Irving.

"Kyrie knows what it takes to win a championship, so as a first-time NBA coach, I'm gonna lean on him in a lot of areas," May told reporters in June.

Still, it's hard to argue that Irving is Dallas' biggest trade asset as the team continues its rebuild. The nine-time All-Star missed the entire 2025-26 season while recovering from a torn ACL, but it can be expected that he's looking to return in top form during the upcoming campaign.

If the Mavs struggle to find success during the start of the 2026-27 season, they could become more open to the idea of trading Irving for the right offer.

articles.title: Angel Reese Breaks 2 WNBA Records, Final Box Score Stats, Highlights as Dream Beat Brink, Sparks
articles.summary: Angel Reese and the Atlanta Dream remain red hot after she broke two WNBA records to lead the team to a 78-71 win over the Los Angeles Sparks.
articles.body:
Angel Reese and the Atlanta Dream remain red hot after she broke two WNBA records to lead the team to a 78-71 win over the Los Angeles Sparks.

The Dream, who were favored by 10.5 points at FanDuel, faced a much bigger test than their last matchup with the Sparks on Aug. 20 that they won by 36 points.

Reese helped them hold off Los Angeles by recording a WNBA single-game record 26 rebounds. She also set a single-season record in total rebounds during the game at 458 with six games remaining in the regular season.

Reese broke the single-season record for total rebounds with 6:17 remaining in the fourth quarter when she grabbed an offensive board off a missed layup. She passed A'ja Wilson's record of 451 set in 2024.

The 26 total rebounds in a game broke the record that had stood for 23 years. Chamique Holdsclaw had held the single-game mark of 24 rebounds since May 23, 2003.

"That's a talent," Dream guard Allisha Gray said of Reese after the win. "I'm just in awe watching her rebound."

This marks the second consecutive game against the Sparks in which Reese has made WNBA history. Her previous outing four days ago saw her become the first player to have at least 20 points, 10 rebounds, five assists and three steals without missing a shot.

Reese has led the Dream (25-13) to four consecutive wins and six victories in their last seven games. They remain in the No. 4 spot in the playoff race, just one-half game behind the Las Vegas Aces for the three seed.

Atlanta is off until Friday when it will host the Connecticut Sun before the WNBA takes a three-week break for the FIBA World Cup.

articles.title: Más equipos grandes y mercados claves se comprometen para ser franquicias de la Euroliga
articles.standfirst: Recibe más de una docena de ofertas vinculantes de equipos para convertirse en franquicias que generarán más de 700 millones e inversiones de 3.200 millones en infraestructuras
articles.summary: Recibe más de una docena de ofertas vinculantes de equipos para convertirse en franquicias que generarán más de 600 millones e inversiones de 2.000 millones en infraestructuras
articles.body: El Board de la Euroliga celebrado esta mañana en Barcelona y que contó con la presencia de todos los representantes de equipos accionistas de la competición, anunció a bombo y platillo su imparable plan de expansión con el que lleva camino de monopolizar el baloncesto europeo, tomando una ventaja considerable sobre el proyecto de la NBA Europa cuyo estreno en principio está previsto para la temporada 2027-28. El CEO de la Euroliga, Chus Bueno, dio a conocer con luz y taquígrafos la recepción de más de una docena de ofertas vinculantes, con compromisos ya firmados, de equipos e inversores que han demostrado con documentos rubricados su deseo de convertirse en franquicias de la Euroliga a partir de la temporada 2027-28, en la que el torneo probablemente cambiará de formato y será dividido en dos Conferencias, ante el crecimiento del número de equipos. Esas ofertas vinculantes garantizan a la competición unos ingresos de más de 700 millones de euros sumando el canon -de diversa cuantía en función de su trascendencia en el mercado baloncestístico continental- que tendrán que abonar entre todos los nuevos socios, contratos vinculantes de varios equipos y ciudades entre los que se encuentran Valencia Basket, Dubai Basketball, PAOK Salónica, París Basketball, Hapoel Tel Aviv, Partizan o Estrella Roja. Además, añade a su imparable expansión nuevas ciudades muy estratégicos como Londres, Roma y Nápoles con los que la Euroliga consigue afianzar y proteger los siete mercados más importantes del baloncesto europeo: Turquía, Grecia, Italia, España, Alemania, Francia y Gran Bretaña. Amplía así sus fronteras, gana terreno en todo el baloncesto europeo y refuerza su dominio. Todos estos equipos y ciudades demuestran con sus ofertas vinculantes estar totalmente comprometidos e ilusionados con este proyecto, como prueba el hecho de que además de aportar entre todos ellos más de 700 millones de euros como canon, invertirán más de 3.200 millones de euros en infraestructuras. Todos estos nuevos equipos e inversores han pasado ya el primer 'due diligence' del Board de la Euroliga, un proceso de investigación, revisión y comprobación para constatar que tienen capacidad y son suficientemente solventes y competitivos para poder convertirse en franquicias de la competición. Aunque la aprobación final será en el Board of Owners o Asamblea de Dueños que tendrá lugar a finales de este próximo mes de septiembre y del que saldrán las nuevas franquicias cuyas propuestas sean aceptadas. Chus Bueno, que tomó las riendas de la Euroliga como nuevo CEO el 30 de enero de 2026, y su equipo ejecutivo han logrado en apenas ocho meses que el proyecto de la Euroliga siga avanzando a pasos agigantados con su ambicioso plan de expansión que parece no tener techo, logrando un crecimiento exponencial desde el punto de vista cuantitativo y cualitativo que le permite consolidar su dominio en el mercado del baloncesto europeo.      “La Euroliga está experimentando un fuerte impulso, tanto a nivel comercial como estratégico, con importantes renovaciones de acuerdos de colaboración a largo plazo acordadas en las últimas semanas y el lanzamiento de nuevos eventos que continúan expandiendo nuestra plataforma", explicó Bueno. El CEO de la Euroliga destacó también la consolidación del proyecto: "Al mismo tiempo, el interés que ha despertado el proceso de franquicias refleja claramente la confianza que clubes, inversores y nuevos proyectos depositan en el futuro de la Euroliga. Las ofertas vinculantes, cercanas a los 700 millones de euros, que representan una inversión total de más de 3.200 millones de euros en los próximos cinco años, demuestran la solidez de nuestro modelo de negocio y el valor que se genera en toda la Liga". Una inversión de los clubes que redundará íntegramente en ellos mismos, no en la organización. La Euroliga ha exigido a todos esos inversores su compromiso por escrito con el dinero que va a ser adelantado por los clubes para los propios clubes. Y esa es la premisa que más y mejor estimula el compromiso y la ilusión de todos ellos de apostar por una competición de la que los propios clubes serán los únicos beneficiarios.

articles.summary: The Golden State Warriors have signed free agent guard Brandon Williams to a one-year, $2.6 million contract, according to ESPN's Shams Charania.
articles.body:
The Golden State Warriors have signed free agent guard Brandon Williams to a one-year, $2.6 million contract, according to ESPN's Shams Charania.

Here's a look at the team's current active roster and salary cap situation.

Per Spotrac , the Warriors had roughly $249.4 million allocated toward the 2026-27 salary cap before landing Williams, which will now put them at about $252 million. They are now below the second apron threshold by about $2.6 million.

Williams, 26, is a 6'1" guard who has played four NBA seasons. He played 24 games (16 starts) with the 2021-22 Portland Trail Blazers but didn't see any NBA action in 2022-23. That year, Williams played for the G League's College Park Skyhawks.

Williams has also suited up for the G League's Westchester Knicks (2021-22) and Osceola Magic (2023).

In Dec. 2023, Williams signed a two-way deal with the Dallas Mavericks. He's played 116 games over three seasons with the Mavs, including 66 in 2023-24 (15 starts).

He averaged 13.0 points, 3.9 assists and 2.9 rebounds over 22.2 minutes per game last season.

Earlier in August, NBA insider Marc Stein reported that the Warriors were interested in Williams and forward Georges Niang for their remaining open roster spots.

In the end, Golden State added Williams to the roster as the team hopes to make the playoffs after an injury-plagued 2025-26 season ended one game short of that feat after a loss to the Phoenix Suns in the Western Conference play-in tournament.

articles.title: Breaking Down NBA 2K27's Best New Features for This Year's Game
articles.summary: NBA 2K27 is nearly here, and this year's entry sees the game's developers continue to provide the most realistic, authentic on-court experience for die-hard basketball fans while also enhancing the off-the-court options for the casual audience.
articles.body:
NBA 2K27 is nearly here, and this year's entry sees the game's developers continue to provide the most realistic, authentic on-court experience for die-hard basketball fans while also enhancing the off-the-court options for the casual audience.

Significant attention was paid to improving gameplay while also introducing a first-time-ever element to its popular The City mode.

Dive deeper into each of those in this breakdown of the new features.

Date: August 26 (Deluxe and Ultra editions), September 4 (Standard edition)

Platforms: PlayStation 5, Xbox Series X/S, Stream for PC, and Nintendo Switch 2

Cover Athletes: Victor Wembanyama (Standard), Caitlin Clark (Deluxe), Derrick Rose (Ultra)

2K has committed to bringing the most authentic NBA experience to gamers with this year's release by adding several new features to the gameplay engine.

Now players can make like Anthony Edwards and use the step-up up-and-unders to create separation and knock down game-sealing shots.

Expanded dribbling customization lets gamers add every element of a player's offensive attack to their arsenal, and a new layup tool prevents the ball from clipping parts of the rim or backboard.

A new timing- and logic-based dunk meter tightens when a defender confronts you at or near the rim, and rhythm shooting is upgraded.

Perhaps most interesting is the introduction of a more physical defense.

2K has made sure to emphasize an element of the game that may not be as omnipresent on the hardwood as some would like by making considerable upgrades to the defensive side of the ball.

Defensive cutoffs and a new collision system make offenses choose the right moves at the right times or face potential blocked shots and turnovers.

For the first time in NBA 2K history, male and female MyPLAYERS can play together in The City.

There will be thousands of options to outfit both men and women. More importantly, all modes within The City will be co-ed.

The game's official website notes that female MyPLAYERS are exclusive to The City, though.
